The sun went down in red and gold,
watched it from the hill, .
With purple clouds like banners rolled,
Whose tips are rosy still.
Where are the eyes that oft of old
Have watched in veal or woe,
While the sun set in red and gold,
thousand years agoY
A linnet perched upon the bush,
And sang in thrilling strain,
Dueting with his neighbor thrush,
Till the air thrilled again;
And all the wood with music rang,
Their voices echoed So
Who listened while the linnet sang
A thousand years ago?
Where are they-all those beating hearts
That lived and throbbed like ours,
Who acted out their separate parts,
And used their varied powers?
The hearts that gazed, and thrilled, and


burned,


And writhed in PASSIONS glow,
Or with the tenderest pity yearned
thousand years agoS'
Where are they ?-haply over some
The "dust to dust" was said,
Who slumber each in ballowed tomb,
Till angels wake the dead,
Some linger in the dreamless sleep
In oceans coral caves;
And mighty fragrant forests weep
Their dew on others graves.
But all their souls, we must be sure,
The grave can never hold
The immortal essence will endure


When hearts and hands grow cold.
They may be floating round us now,
Above us and beneath,
The very breeze that fans our brow
May be spirits breath.
doubt not but they mark with sighs
Our faults and follies all;
Oh sad to think some spirits eyes
Grow DINNER when we fall.
Like us the end of time they walt,


Their final doom to know,
Whatever was their earthly state


A thousand years ago.

The winds and rams have stormed gou..
They wrestled with the struggling trees,
And now weird, wild moan


Watts softly on the breeze.
thousand rain-drops from the leaves
Are trickling to the turf below,
While strange sunlight weaves
Where the pale asters glow.
Wrenched by the fiery, iron arm
OF frowning tempest the young oak
Has felt the fatal harm,


Has fallen with the stroke.
Sad is the green and splntered stem,
And sad the crushed and clustering sprays
In all the grove, gem,


Now corse.l like, it decays.
view the change of outward form
The guiding, master hand beneath
! shudder at the storm


weep its work of death.
Why weep, when every shelving hill,
And every moorland stretching far,
Hath oak and hemiock still,
Hath sun and hower.star?
Why weep? A part of me is dead;
For though the world is thronged with men,
This oak whose lie is fed


Recalls his death again.
For had learned to prize his worth,
His feeling heart and sturdy mlnd
His mild and genial mirth,


His purposes refined.
But they are gone! l feel the wound
Not long knew, but loved him well,
For love is ever found


Where truth and meekness dwell
A sunlight falls within the void
On virtues not so bright before
/ mourn the oak destroyed,


The bloom prize the more.
The yellow soil is loose and bare
That heaped upon his manly breast,
In shower and summer air


Shall yet be freshly dressed,
With raiment of the grassy spire,
Inwoven with the latest flowers,
All early to expire


In autumns frosty hours.
A symbol of his few green years,


That, IN their growing beauty, met
The eath-blight-leaving tears


And many vain regret.

Long years of sorrow, joy and pain
That prattling boy to man has grown,

1t is with an i'll grace that evil words are


spoken OF the dead. None of us will ever for.

lived she was terror and a monster, who dealt
in death as a pastime, and poisoned babes in
order that she might judge The effect her drugs
would have on adults. Now she is dead all
are disposed TO let her sleep we'll While she

woman, the crowd would have torn her limb
from limb if they could have laid their hands on
her. NOW she has met her DOOM none would
dlsnonor her bones, even If the hidden grave in
which she sleeps were revealed.


In the murder OF Mary Caroline Caruthers we
all thought that the fendishness of the Borgia
mad reached its saddest elimination. Young
woman--a bride, just commencing happy life
under the most genial circumstances; beautiful
10 such degree that she caused the universal
admiration even of her own sex; as good as she
was beautiful; happy wife and beloved
daughter blessing an unshadowed home such
woman was 1t that Martha Grinder murdered
Win tne cold,blooded malignity OF q 6end, that
few household articles and little money
might fall to the murderess. She murdered
her, too, with sucl, needless torture, PLAYING
with her victims misery. and laughing-one
can imagine, half regretfully-when the last
scene came, and the poor girl lay dead.


All this was bad enough, but Martha Grinder
did worse. Mary Caruthers had husband,
young, vigorous, happy, and prosperous. The
eEb one VINO murdered MS Vile worse than
murdered him. For every dose of poison she
gave his wife, she gave one to him, hoping to
Kill them both. The delicate woman died, the
more stalwart man lived, wretched wreck.
The terrible desth OF his wife left his home desc
late, his life darkeneG, als future blank. The
poison his enemy had fed rim continued It's fell
work long after the murderess was Eouldering
in her felon's grave. 1t had shattered every.
nerve, and had wrecked every joint, Grief
stricken: with his memories saddened BY the
blight that had withered his life; with every
hope dead; with terrible physical suffering
added daily and nightly to mental anguish, and
yet too strong to die-what else but one thing
Thursday last James Caruthers was taken a
hopeless lunatlc from his home in New Castle to
Dixmont Hospital,


To our minds, this crime for which Martha
Grinder did not die, and which she was uncon-
scious, for the most part, of having committed,
is the most terrible of all her terrible list. If
anything could make us think our charity for
the dead sinner a superstition and lead us to
curse the memory OF the coffined wretch, this
proof Of how the crime reaches out active and
potent, after the criminal is only dust, would
do it. Verify, the evil that she did lives after
her.-Plttsburg Gazette. -

steamer Missouri left New Orleans last Tuesday
week, with light freight, but full of passengers,

When woman, by her idle loom,
Heard the dread battles nearing boom
With clasped hands and straining ear;
While each new hour the past pursues


With further threat of loss and pain,
Till the sick senses would refuse
To longer drink the bloody news

The days of calm at length are won,


And, sitting thus, with folded hands,
We talk Of great deeds greatly done,
While all the future seems to run

And while new shrines to Peace we build,
On our great banners azure field

Who bore the flag-who won the day?


The young, proud manhood of the land,
Called from the forge and plough away,

With eager but untutored hand;
They swarmed o'er all the roads that led


To where the peril hottest burned.
By night, by day, their hurrying tread

Why tell how long the contest hung,

No more the dreaded stretchers drip,


The jolting ambulances grOan;

We hear from the soon silent lip

And ye who on the seas blue breast,

On Tuesday night, says the ST. Louis
Democrat of May 5th, number of guests
assembled on Sixteenth street to witness a
marriage ceremony. The wedding feast was
spread-the priest came with his cross and
prayer book-the groomsmen assembled in
their white kids and paper shirt collars
the bridemaids were present with their
founces and globular waterfalls-the bride,
blushing like Aurora, was arrayed in snowy
robes, orange wreaths and glittering jewels
the wedding ring was ready, and every
thing was prepared to launch the young
couple upon the Hymenial stream, amid re-
joicings, flowers, kisses, tears, tremors and
congratulations.


Only one thing was needed to make the
thing complete, and that was the presence
ofthe bridegroom. Without him the play
would be like the play of Hamlet with Ham
let left out In fact he was an indispensa-
BILE character, and without his presence the
whole affair must fall through and prove
failure. But, important as was his presence,
the appointed bridegroom came not.


Hours passed. The priest became dis
gusted and left-the uncle ofthe bride grew
red in the face-the groomsmen looked
sour-the bridesmaids languished-and the
bride grew nervous and pale. Still the lag
gard fingered. Midnight approached
The hoarse clarion of the ancient shanghai
in the yard, announced the approach of the
" we sma' hours" and still no bridegroom
appeared. The supper got cold-the uncle
was in towering passion-the bridesmaids
wept-the groomsmen went to bed.


A committee was sent to look after the
recusant lover, and after visiting his mar
BILE drug store and not finding him there,
they went to his room and found him
ssOeetly sleeping." He was aroused from
his slumber and hurried off to the brides
house.


When he arrived there the guests were
gone. He gave as an excuse that, feelin g
unwell, he had taken dose of morphine,
and had oversight himself, but was now
willing to face the music and go through
the trying ordeal By this time the native
pride of the fair bride was aroused, and the
sleepy gentlemen was informed that the
wedding was indefinitely postponed.


The bridegroom returned to his pestle
and mortar and the young lady remains at
home fair ungathered flower. 1t was
near approach to wedding, but a miss
is as good as a mile"
